title: De motu vibratorio laminarum elasticarum, ubi plures novae vibrationum species hactenus non pertractatae evolvuntur

deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler is deriving the equation of transverse vibration of an elastic lamina (beam). On the previous page he applied d'Alembert's principle: each element dx at abscissa x carries the reversed inertial force p dx = (K dx/2bk)(∂²y/∂t²). Equilibrium of the free portion FY about the point Y then requires that the moment of these forces equal the elastic moment Kcc(∂²y/∂x²).

On this page he computes that moment. Fix the point Y with abscissa x. Let a running point y have abscissa X, with 0 ≤ X ≤ x, measured from the free end F/B. The force P dX acting at that point has lever arm (x − X) about Y. Its moment is P dX (x − X). Integrating gives M = x∫P dX − ∫P X dX, with the integrals taken so that they vanish at X = 0. Setting the upper limit X = x and P = p gives

M(x) = x∫₀ˣ p dX − ∫₀ˣ p X dX = ∫₀ˣ dx ∫₀ˣ p dx.

This is the n = 2 case of the repeated-integration (Cauchy) formula: M′ = ∫p, and M″ = p. Substituting p gives

M = (K/2bk) ∫dx ∫dx (∂²y/∂t²).

Both the single and the double integral must vanish at x = 0, because no forces act beyond the free end F. In modern terms, shear force and bending moment are zero at a free end, i.e. y_xx = y_xxx = 0 there.

On the next page, after a sign argument, M is equated to the elastic moment and differentiated twice. The result is the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation y_tt = −b⁴ y_xxxx, with b⁴ = 2bkcc.
errors: The scan prints the moment as 'P x X . X x = P dX (x − X)'. The first factor should be the force P dX, not 'P xX', so this is apparently a misprint in the original. The right-hand side is correct.

No mathematical error. The identity x∫p dx − ∫p x dx = ∫dx∫p dx holds when both integrals vanish at 0. The sign of the acceleration is deferred to the next page and handled there by a physical argument.

ideas.what: Bending moment at a section obtained as the integral of a distributed load times its lever arm (x − X). This is reduced to an iterated double integral, with the free-end conditions that the integrals vanish at x = 0.
ideas.modern_name: Moment–load relation M'' = q; Cauchy formula for repeated integration (n = 2); free-end conditions on shear and moment
ideas.usually_credited_to: Beam statics: Jacob Bernoulli, Euler, Daniel Bernoulli (1730s–1740s). Repeated-integration formula: Cauchy (1823), though the n = 2 identity was folklore earlier.
ideas.where_published: Euler's earlier elastic-lamina vibration work (E40, Comm. Acad. Petrop. 1735/1740; the 1744 Methodus inveniendi, Additamentum I) and E443 itself

ideas.what: Use of d'Alembert's principle: inertial forces are treated as applied loads in a static moment balance for a vibrating beam, leading to the fourth-order PDE.
ideas.modern_name: Derivation of the Euler–Bernoulli dynamic beam equation
ideas.where_published: E40; correspondence with Daniel Bernoulli; Methodus inveniendi (1744); Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies (1960)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard, correct derivation of the bending moment as a double integral of the inertial load. It is well documented in Truesdell's history of Euler's beam theory and has nothing new.
transcription_corrections: 'P xX. Xx = P dX (x − X)' faithfully reproduces the printed misprint. The intended expression is 'P dX . Xx = P dX (x − X)'.
'euaneſcente abſciſſa Bx = X ſimul euaneſcat' is correct, with 'abſciſſa' printed with a long-s ligature.
